I read the csv file like this:
dfs <- read.csv ("dfs.csv", colClasses = c("factor", "numeric", "factor", "factor", "numeric"))
I want to compare the mean measured values of each time point to time = 0 for each gene and each line
i.e. something like this :
with (dfs, t.test(meas[time==0], meas[time==4]))
I've grouped the df by genes, line, time and it seems like summarise should do the trick but I can't make it work.

Thanks in advance for your help and time!!!

messages.author: 0c0915d54307a5d8
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: t.test
parts:
Doing multiple t-tests on the same data set is usually frowned upon. Is there some reason why you want to compare each of the time points to zero and not do a linear model using all the time points? That would look like this:

m1 = glm(meas ~ time, data = dfs)
summary(m1)

# If you want all the comparisons, you can always just do an ANOVA and a post-hoc to get the comparisons of each time step
# to zero (and to each of the other time steps). This would be more appropriate than a t-test for each time point.
dfs$time2 = as.factor(dfs$time)
m2 = aov(meas ~ time2, data = dfs)
summary(m2)
TukeyHSD(m2)

# if you want it in a table, the plyr package may be your friend
library(plyr)
dfs2 = ddply(dfs, .(Genes, time), summarize, mmeas = mean(meas))

That should give you a new data frame with the mean of the measurement for each time point. Hope that helps!

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: t.test
parts:
Well, you could try this:

# load the plyr library
library(plyr)

# Group your data by gene and line, then do an ANOVA on each group.
 dfs3 = daply(dfs, .(Genes, line), function(x) {
   a1 = aov(meas~time2, data=x)

# Do a Tukey post-hoc on the ANOVA
   p= TukeyHSD(a1)

# return just the p-values for each time period versus the 0 time point.
   return(p$time2[1:4, 4])
 })

My solution doesn't use t-tests, but you end up doing fewer hypothesis tests overall, which is generally considered better.

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: t.test
parts:
Hi Sharon,

*Edited to clarify some points

You can still apply a linear model/classical ANOVA to these data by treating the times as categorical data rather than continuous. This is preferable to running separate models because of the issue of multiple comparisons (Rosemary's solution would still suffer this - _ed. I did not see that time2 is a factor, however, the issue with multiple comparisons arises from running a separate model for each gene. It would be better to model all genes simultaneously._ ). 

I would suggest something like: 

my_model<-aov(meas ~ factor(time),data=dfs)

TukeyHSD(my_model)

A different means comparison might also be warranted if your "control" is time = 0 and you only care about comparisons between time !=0 and time = 0. 
 
Hope that helps,

Matt

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: t.test
parts:
Hi Sharon,

The reason to model all genes simultaneously is to avoid finding significance in what is really just noise. Simply, the more things you measure the greater likelihood some will look significant when they are not. The means comparison methods are calibrated to control this compounding error rate, but this goes out the window when you are running hundreds or thousands of models. Without knowing your data better, I would say that different responses do not necessarily ensure independence. 

My little bit of code just showed how to run the times as a category. Looking a bit more carefully at your data, it appears you have some additional structure in your data (reps). To get a functional model for this is a bit more involved if your times are grouped.

There are some pretty slick packages for modeling genomic data that enforce some level of sparsity (thereby control error rates). I don't do genomic work, so can cannot name any off hand, but I know this is the type of work that Dr. Dan Runcie does. I am sure there are some people on this list that also could help with this.

Matt
